passages.title: The Dragon's Riddle
passages.text: 'I am the one thing that grows smaller the more of me you take, and larger the more of me you leave behind,' the dragon intoned, its voice like pages turning in a vast and ancient book. The apprentice hesitated. To answer wrongly was to forfeit her memories; to refuse was to forfeit the library. She thought of the corridors she had walked that morning, each one stretching further behind her. 'Footsteps,' she whispered. The dragon's eyes narrowed — not, she realised, in anger, but in something perilously close to delight.

passages.title: The Ferryman

The translator is less a bridge-builder than a ferryman who must decide, with each crossing, which cargo can survive the water.

passages.title: From Access to Discernment

passages.title: The Unfinished Index
passages.text: When the old librarian died, she left behind an index of the Starlight Library that ran to forty volumes and was, by her own admission, incomplete. Her successor proposed to finish it. Within a year he had abandoned the project, not for lack of diligence but because he had grasped what she had always known: an index of a living library can never be finished, since every entry alters the meaning of those around it. A book catalogued under 'Astronomy' in one decade migrates, in the next, to 'Myth'. To index, he wrote, is not to record knowledge but to take a position on it, and positions, unlike shelves, do not stay put.

passages.title: On Translation
passages.text: It is often said that translation is a kind of betrayal, and the Italian pun 'traduttore, traditore' ('translator, traitor') is cited as proof. But the charge assumes that an original possesses a single, fixed meaning which the translator either preserves or corrupts. Few writers would recognise their work in that description. A poem's meaning lives partly in its sounds, its rhythms and the associations its words carry for a particular audience at a particular time; none of these can survive the journey into another language intact. The honest translator does not pretend otherwise. She makes choices, sacrifices one quality to save another, and in doing so produces not a copy but a reading: a version that may, on occasion, illuminate what the original concealed.

passages.title: The Apprentice of the Starlight Library
passages.text: Nobody had told Ilse that the Starlight Library rearranged itself at midnight. On her first night as apprentice, she watched, aghast, as the shelves of astronomy slid silently into the poetry wing and a whole staircase folded itself into a cupboard. The Head Librarian, unperturbed, merely remarked that the library 'preferred to be read rather than searched'. Only weeks later did Ilse grasp what he meant: whenever she stopped hunting for a particular book and simply wandered, the book she needed would, as often as not, find its way into her hands. She came to suspect that the library was less a building than a temperament.

passages.title: On Being Wrong
passages.text: There is a peculiar pleasure, rarely acknowledged, in discovering that one has been wrong. Admittedly, the pleasure arrives late; the first sensation is closer to embarrassment. But once the sting fades, what remains is a world that has become slightly larger and more interesting than the one we had imagined. Scientists, at their best, cultivate this feeling deliberately, framing each experiment as an attempt to prove themselves mistaken. The rest of us might do well to follow suit, not least because those who can never admit error tend to stop learning altogether.

passages.title: The Clockmaker's Riddle
passages.text: When old Master Varga died, he left his workshop not to his son, as everyone had assumed, but to whichever of his three apprentices could repair the great astronomical clock in the town square, which had been silent for forty years. Two of them set to work at once, dismantling the mechanism with feverish haste. The third, a quiet girl named Dora, spent the first week merely watching the clock, notebook in hand. It was she who noticed that the hands had not seized at all; they had been deliberately locked by a tiny brass pin, placed there, it later emerged, by Varga himself, so that only someone patient enough to look before touching would ever find it.

passages.title: Should Robots Have Rights?
passages.text: The question sounds absurd until one considers how readily children form attachments to robotic pets, mourning them when they break and protesting when adults treat them roughly. Some philosophers argue that the issue is not whether machines can suffer, which for now they almost certainly cannot, but what our treatment of them says about us. If kicking a lifelike robot dog makes cruelty feel normal, the argument runs, then perhaps we should discourage it, not for the robot's sake but for ours. Critics counter that this risks muddling our moral priorities when real animals still suffer neglect.

passages.title: The Last Speaker of the Whistled Language
passages.text: On the steep island of La Gomera, shepherds once communicated across deep ravines by whistling: not a simple code, but a full version of Spanish in which tones and pitches stand in for vowels and consonants. By the 1990s, the language, known as Silbo, was on the verge of extinction, kept alive by a dwindling number of elderly whistlers. Its revival owes much to an unlikely decision: in 1999, the island made Silbo compulsory in primary schools. Today, schoolchildren whistle their homework answers, and the language has been recognised by UNESCO as part of the world's cultural heritage. Whether it will survive as more than a classroom curiosity, however, remains an open question.

passages.title: Notes from a Reluctant Debater
passages.text: I joined the debate club under duress, my form tutor having decided that my habit of arguing with everyone might as well be put to some use. What I hadn't bargained for was being made to argue, week after week, for positions I found indefensible. The first time I had to defend the idea that homework should be doubled, I could barely keep a straight face. Yet somewhere along the way, a disconcerting thing happened: I began to understand, if not agree with, people I had previously dismissed. Being forced to build the strongest case for the other side, it turns out, is the surest way of discovering the weaknesses in your own.

passages.title: The Cartographer's Daughter
passages.text: Maps, her father liked to say, were not pictures of the world but arguments about it. Every map decided what mattered: which rivers were named, which villages vanished beneath a convenient blank. As a child, Mira had thought this a pleasantly eccentric remark. Only when she began drawing maps of her own did its full weight settle on her. To map the forest behind her house, she had to decide whether the badgers' sett deserved a symbol, whether the path the dog-walkers had worn counted as a path at all. Each choice, she realised, quietly told the reader what to notice and what to ignore.

passages.title: In Defence of the Unfinished
passages.text: We revere the completed work: the published novel, the polished symphony. Yet history is littered with masterpieces that were never finished, from Schubert's 'Unfinished' Symphony to Gaudí's still-rising basilica, and their incompleteness is often part of their power. An unfinished work invites the audience in; it asks us to imagine what might have been. There is a lesson here for anyone paralysed by perfectionism. The draft abandoned in a drawer achieves nothing, but the half-built project shared with others can inspire, provoke and, occasionally, be completed by hands other than our own.

passages.title: The Lost Hour
passages.text: Each spring, when the clocks went forward, Grandpa Tobias insisted that the missing hour had not vanished but merely been 'mislaid', and that it could be found by anyone sufficiently determined. My cousins and I spent years searching: under floorboards, inside the grandfather clock, in the pages of his oldest books. It was not until after his death that we found, tucked inside his watch, a note in his spidery hand: 'The hour was always in the searching. Thank you for spending it with me.' We wept, of course; but we also laughed, for we understood at last that we had been not detectives but guests.

questions.explain: 'Tucked inside his watch.'

notes.under a floorboard: They searched there, but didn't find it.
notes.in a book: They searched books, but the note was in the watch.

questions.q: What did the note reveal?
options: that he had lied to them
that the hour was in the clock
questions.explain: 'The hour was always in the searching.'

notes.that he had lied to them: It reframes, not confesses a lie.

questions.q: What does 'not detectives but guests' mean?
options: they had failed to solve a crime
questions.explain: The searching was time spent together, like guests at his invitation.

passages.title: Can Animals Be Bored?
passages.text: Anyone who has watched a caged parrot pluck out its own feathers may suspect that animals experience something like boredom. Proving it is another matter. In one study, mink kept in bare cages were found to spend more time lying awake but inactive, and, crucially, to investigate any new object, even unpleasant ones, far more eagerly than mink in enriched enclosures. Researchers argue that this hunger for stimulation, regardless of its quality, is precisely what boredom looks like. If they are right, the implications for how we house farm, zoo and even pet animals are considerable.

questions.q: What does the parrot example suggest?
questions.explain: It 'may suspect that animals experience something like boredom'.

questions.q: What does 'Proving it is another matter' mean?
questions.explain: Suspecting is easy; proving is much harder.

questions.q: What did mink in bare cages do?
questions.explain: 'Investigate any new object… far more eagerly.'

questions.q: Why is 'even unpleasant ones' important?
options: it shows they wanted any stimulation
it shows they liked unpleasant things
it proves the cages were dirty
questions.explain: A 'hunger for stimulation, regardless of its quality'.

notes.it shows they liked unpleasant things: They wanted stimulation, not unpleasantness itself.

questions.q: What does the final sentence suggest?
questions.explain: 'The implications for how we house… animals are considerable.'

passages.title: The Echo Chamber Problem
passages.text: Recommendation algorithms are designed to show us more of what we already like, which sounds harmless enough. Over time, however, they can narrow our horizons without our noticing: the music fan who once explored widely finds her playlist shrinking to a single genre; the curious reader is offered only opinions that echo his own. The danger is not that algorithms lie, but that they flatter. Some designers now build in deliberate 'serendipity', occasionally slipping in something unexpected. Whether users will tolerate being surprised, rather than pleased, remains to be seen.

questions.q: What are recommendation algorithms designed to do?
options: show us more of what we like
questions.explain: 'Designed to show us more of what we already like.'

notes.challenge our opinions: That's what serendipity tries to add.

questions.q: What is the gradual effect described?
questions.explain: 'Narrow our horizons without our noticing.'

notes.we stop listening to music: The playlist shrinks, but she still listens.

questions.q: What does 'they flatter' mean here?
questions.explain: Flattering = pleasing us by confirming our views, unlike lying.

questions.q: What is 'serendipity' in this context?
options: a new type of algorithm error
questions.explain: 'Occasionally slipping in something unexpected' on purpose.

questions.q: What uncertainty does the writer end with?
questions.explain: 'Whether users will tolerate being surprised, rather than pleased.'

passages.title: The Girl Who Talked to Glaciers
passages.text: Freya had grown up beside the Sólheimajökull glacier, and in her family it was a standing joke that she spoke to it each morning. What began as a childish game became, by the age of fifteen, a meticulous diary: every day she photographed the glacier's edge from the same rock and recorded the distance to a marker her grandfather had painted decades earlier. Her photographs, posted online, attracted the attention of a university team, who found that her amateur record was more continuous than their own. The glacier, she says, has retreated nearly a kilometre in her lifetime. 'I used to talk to it. Now I feel I'm keeping it company.'

questions.q: How did her family see her habit at first?
questions.explain: 'It was a standing joke.'

questions.q: What does 'meticulous' tell us about her diary?
options: it was very careful and precise
it was written in a hurry
questions.explain: Same rock, daily photos, measured distances = meticulous.

questions.q: What did she use as a reference point?
questions.explain: 'A marker her grandfather had painted decades earlier.'

questions.q: Why was her record valuable to the scientists?
options: it had fewer gaps than theirs
questions.explain: 'More continuous than their own.'

questions.q: What does her final remark suggest?
options: she no longer cares about it
she hopes it will grow back soon
she wants to leave the area
questions.explain: 'Keeping it company' as it retreats suggests loyalty and sadness.

passages.title: The Clockwork Nightingale
passages.text: The emperor's new nightingale was, by every measurable standard, superior to the old one. It never tired, never sang off-key and could perform the same twelve melodies with flawless precision for as long as anyone cared to listen. The court was enchanted; the real bird, a drab little thing that sang only when it felt like it, was quietly forgotten and flew back to the forest. It was not until the mechanism wound down one winter's night, and the palace fell utterly silent, that anyone noticed what had been lost. The clockwork bird had never once surprised them. The real one, whose songs no one could predict, had done so every single evening.

questions.q: How is the clockwork bird presented in the first two sentences?
options: deeply moving to everyone who heard it
questions.explain: 'By every measurable standard, superior… flawless precision.'

notes.deeply moving to everyone who heard it: The story suggests it moved no one in the end.

questions.q: What does 'by every measurable standard' imply?
options: the old bird was better in every way
questions.explain: The phrase hints that unmeasurable qualities, like surprise, are what matter.

notes.the old bird was better in every way: The new bird was better on measured points.

questions.q: What happened to the real bird?
options: it was put in a cage
it was given to the forest by the emperor
questions.explain: 'Quietly forgotten and flew back to the forest.'

notes.it was given to the forest by the empero: It flew back on its own.

questions.q: What finally made the court realise their mistake?
options: the real nightingale's sudden return to the palace
questions.explain: 'Not until the mechanism wound down… and the palace fell utterly silent.'

notes.the real nightingale's sudden return to: The bird doesn't come back in this passage.
notes.a broken melody: It stopped completely; it didn't play wrongly.

questions.q: What is the passage's central contrast?
options: the cold of winter versus the warmth of summer
questions.explain: 'Never once surprised them… had done so every single evening.'

passages.title: On the Tyranny of the High Score
passages.text: Few inventions have been as quietly influential as the high-score table. Before it appeared, a game was simply played; afterwards, it was played against everyone who had ever played it before. The effect on players was, and remains, double-edged. On one hand, the scoreboard turned a solitary pastime into a kind of conversation across time, the initials of strangers taunting or inspiring you. On the other, it introduced a nagging sense that no performance, however enjoyable, was quite good enough. Anyone who has abandoned a perfectly pleasant game the moment it became clear that no record was within reach will recognise the problem. The score, designed to measure the fun, had begun to replace it.

questions.q: What changed, according to the writer, when high scores appeared?
options: games became much shorter and simpler to finish
questions.explain: 'Played against everyone who had ever played it before.'

notes.people stopped playing alone: It felt like a 'conversation', but they still played alone.

questions.q: What does 'double-edged' mean here?
questions.explain: The writer gives 'on one hand… on the other'.

notes.affecting two players: It isn't about the number of players.

questions.q: What positive effect is described?
options: a sense of connection with other players
far more realistic and colourful graphics
questions.explain: 'A kind of conversation across time, the initials of strangers taunting or inspiring you.'

questions.q: What does the example of abandoning a game illustrate?
options: the game itself was badly designed and dull
questions.explain: 'Abandoned a perfectly pleasant game the moment… no record was within reach.'

notes.players get bored quickly: They quit because of the score, not boredom.
notes.records are easy to beat: The record was out of reach.

questions.q: What is ironic about the final sentence?
options: a measure of fun replaced the fun
high-score tables were never actually popular with players
questions.explain: 'The score, designed to measure the fun, had begun to replace it.'

passages.title: The Book That Wrote Back
passages.text: On the third evening of her apprenticeship, Ilse discovered that one book in the Starlight Library answered back. She had scribbled a question in its margin – a habit the Head Librarian deplored – and by morning a reply had appeared beneath it in faded violet ink. The reply was, admittedly, not an answer. It was another question, sharper than her own. Over the following weeks, a curious correspondence developed, the book never once conceding a point, Ilse growing steadily better at asking. When at last she confessed it to the Head Librarian, expecting a reprimand, he merely smiled. 'Ah,' he said. 'So it's chosen you. It did the same to me, a very long time ago.'

questions.q: How did the Head Librarian feel about writing in margins?
options: he did not know about it
questions.explain: 'A habit the Head Librarian deplored.'

questions.q: What did the book's reply consist of?
questions.explain: 'It was another question, sharper than her own.'

questions.q: What does 'never once conceding a point' suggest about the book?
options: it never admitted she was right
it agreed with everything Ilse wrote in the margins
questions.explain: To concede = to admit someone is right.

notes.it lost interest quickly: It went on 'over the following weeks'.

questions.q: What did Ilse gain from the exchange?
questions.explain: 'Ilse growing steadily better at asking.'

questions.q: What does the librarian's reaction imply?
options: the book is a kind of teacher
Ilse would be punished for writing in the books
questions.explain: 'So it's chosen you. It did the same to me.'

passages.title: What the Whales Are Singing
passages.text: Male humpback whales are celebrated for their songs – long, complex sequences that can be heard across many kilometres of ocean. What is less widely known is that these songs behave rather like pop music. Within a population, all males sing broadly the same song, yet that song is constantly evolving, and every so often an entirely new tune sweeps through. Researchers tracking whales in the South Pacific have watched songs spread eastward from Australia, island group by island group, over a period of two years. Quite why whales adopt a novel song so readily remains unclear; one intriguing possibility is that novelty itself is attractive, a preference that will be familiar to anyone who has watched a playground craze come and go.

questions.q: What does the writer compare whale songs to?
options: classical concerts performed by large orchestras
questions.explain: 'These songs behave rather like pop music.'

questions.q: What is true of the song within one group?
options: all males share a song that keeps changing
each male sings his own completely different tune all year
questions.explain: 'All males sing broadly the same song, yet that song is constantly evolving.'

questions.q: How did new songs travel in the South Pacific?
questions.explain: 'Spread eastward from Australia, island group by island group.'

notes.all at once: Group by group, not at once.

questions.q: How certain are scientists about why songs are adopted?
options: they have a theory but no proof
they know exactly why and have proved it in experiments
they have no ideas at all
questions.explain: 'Remains unclear; one intriguing possibility is…'

questions.q: Why does the writer mention a playground craze?
questions.explain: It's an everyday example of novelty being attractive.

notes.to describe whale behaviour exactly: It's a comparison, not a description.

passages.title: The Gracious Loser
passages.text: At the junior chess championship, the final game was decided not by a brilliant sacrifice but by a single careless pawn move in the thirtieth minute. Leila, who had been favourite to win, saw her mistake the instant she let go of the piece. What happened next was, to my mind, more impressive than any checkmate. She did not sulk, nor did she offer the limp, unwilling handshake that losing players so often manage. Instead, she congratulated her opponent warmly and stayed behind to analyse the game with him, pointing out a clever idea of his that even the commentators had missed. Had she won, she would have been a champion; losing as she did, she was something rarer.

questions.q: How was the final decided?
questions.explain: 'Not by a brilliant sacrifice but by a single careless pawn move.'

questions.q: When did Leila realise her mistake?
questions.explain: 'The instant she let go of the piece.'

notes.in the thirtieth move: It was the thirtieth minute, not move.

questions.q: What does the writer imply about most losing players?
questions.explain: 'The limp, unwilling handshake that losing players so often manage.'

questions.q: What did Leila notice in the analysis?
options: a mistake by the commentators' board
questions.explain: 'A clever idea of his that even the commentators had missed.'

questions.q: What does the final sentence suggest?
options: her sportsmanship was worth more than winning
she deserved to win and was unlucky to lose the final
questions.explain: 'Losing as she did, she was something rarer.'

notes.she deserved to win and was unlucky to l: The writer praises how she lost.

passages.title: Slime Moulds: Brainless Problem-Solvers
passages.text: If intelligence requires a brain, then the slime mould Physarum polycephalum ought to be hopeless. It is a single, sprawling cell, bright yellow and faintly unappetising, with no nervous system whatsoever. And yet, placed at the entrance of a maze with food at the exit, it will find the shortest route. In a now-famous experiment, Japanese researchers arranged oat flakes in the pattern of the cities around Tokyo; the mould spread out and then pruned itself into a network strikingly similar to the region's actual railway system, which engineers had taken decades to design. None of this means the mould is 'thinking'. It does, however, oblige us to ask whether our definition of problem-solving has been too narrow.

questions.q: What does the first sentence set up?
options: an expectation the text then challenges
a scientific fact that the writer fully agrees with
questions.explain: 'If intelligence requires a brain… ought to be hopeless. And yet…'

notes.a scientific fact that the writer fully: The writer goes on to question it.
notes.a joke about brains: It's an argument, not a joke.

questions.q: How is the slime mould described?
options: as having a tiny but very efficient brain
questions.explain: 'Bright yellow and faintly unappetising.'

questions.q: What did the oat flake experiment show?
options: the mould made an efficient network
railway engineers had copied the mould's design
questions.explain: 'A network strikingly similar to the region's actual railway system.'

notes.railway engineers had copied the mould's: The engineers came first, over decades.
notes.the railway was badly designed: It matched the railway, suggesting it's good.

questions.q: Why does the writer mention 'decades'?
options: to show how old the mould is
to describe the length of the experiment
questions.explain: Engineers took decades; the mould reached a similar result itself.

questions.q: What is the writer's conclusion?
options: we may need a broader idea of problem-solving
the slime mould is truly thinking, just like an animal with a brain
questions.explain: 'None of this means the mould is "thinking"… whether our definition… has been too narrow.'

notes.the slime mould is truly thinking, just: The writer says it does not mean that.
notes.the experiment was flawed: The experiment is called 'famous', not flawed.

passages.title: The Lighthouse Keeper's Apprentice
passages.text: Old Maren had kept the lighthouse on Gull Rock for fifty years, and she had no intention of being replaced by anyone, least of all a boy of twelve who was frightened of the dark. Tobias, for his part, had not asked to be sent. For the first month, they communicated chiefly in grunts. It was the storm that changed things. With the generator failing and a fishing boat drifting towards the rocks, Maren's hands were shaking too badly to light the old oil lamp, and it was Tobias – trembling, but steady enough – who struck the match. Neither of them mentioned it afterwards. But from that night on, Maren left the door to the lamp room unlocked.

questions.q: How did Maren feel about Tobias's arrival?
questions.explain: 'No intention of being replaced by anyone, least of all a boy of twelve.'

notes.curious: There's no interest in him at first.

questions.q: What does 'Tobias, for his part, had not asked to be sent' suggest?
options: he didn't want to be there either
he had volunteered eagerly for the job at the lighthouse
questions.explain: It mirrors Maren's reluctance: neither chose this.

questions.q: What happened during the storm?
questions.explain: 'It was Tobias… who struck the match.'

notes.the fishing boat sank: The light was lit to save it.
notes.Maren lit the lamp alone: Her hands were shaking too badly.

questions.q: What does the unlocked door symbolise?
options: Maren's growing forgetfulness in her old age
questions.explain: 'Neither mentioned it… But from that night on, Maren left the door… unlocked.'

notes.Maren's growing forgetfulness in her old: It's a deliberate choice 'from that night on'.
notes.Tobias's fear of the dark: It's about her attitude, not his fear.

passages.title: In Defence of the Unanswerable Question
passages.text: Science fairs tend to reward projects with tidy conclusions: a hypothesis, an experiment, a neat graph confirming that plants do indeed grow better in sunlight. There is nothing wrong with this, as far as it goes. But it risks teaching young scientists that a good question is one whose answer is already known. Some of the most valuable projects I have seen ended in genuine bafflement – a student who could not explain why her ants always turned left, another whose ice cubes stubbornly froze faster in warm water. Neither won a prize. Both, I suspect, came closer to real science than the sunlit plants ever did, for science begins precisely where the expected answer fails to arrive.

questions.q: What is the writer's view of projects with tidy conclusions?
questions.explain: 'Nothing wrong with this, as far as it goes. But…'

questions.q: What does the plant example illustrate?
options: an experiment with a predictable result
a surprising discovery that changed the student's mind
questions.explain: 'Confirming that plants do indeed grow better in sunlight.'

questions.q: What do the ants and ice cubes have in common?
options: they both won prizes at the science fair
questions.explain: 'Ended in genuine bafflement… could not explain why.'

questions.q: What does 'stubbornly' add to the ice cube example?
options: the result kept happening against expectation
the student was stubborn and refused to give up
questions.explain: 'Stubbornly' suggests it refused to behave as expected, repeatedly.

notes.the student was stubborn and refused to: It describes the ice, not the student.

questions.q: What is the writer's main argument?
options: real science starts with the unexpected
science fair prizes should be abolished completely
fairs are a waste of time
questions.explain: 'Science begins precisely where the expected answer fails to arrive.'

notes.fairs are a waste of time: The writer values the right projects.

passages.title: The Unreliable Narrator Club
passages.text: Our reading group adopted its rather grand name after a heated argument about a mystery novel told by a cheerful, helpful butler. Half of us had trusted him completely; the other half had smelt a rat by chapter three, noting how often he happened to be just outside a door when something went missing. The final chapter, needless to say, vindicated the sceptics. What fascinated us afterwards was not the twist itself, but how skilfully the author had planted clues in plain sight – clues we had all read and most of us had dismissed. Since then, we have treated every narrator with polite suspicion, which has, admittedly, made our meetings longer, if rather more entertaining.

questions.q: How did the club get its name?
options: from a disagreement about a book
questions.explain: 'Adopted its rather grand name after a heated argument about a mystery novel.'

questions.q: What made some readers suspicious of the butler?
questions.explain: 'How often he happened to be just outside a door when something went missing.'

notes.he disappeared in chapter three: Chapter three is when they became suspicious.

questions.q: What does 'vindicated the sceptics' mean?
questions.explain: To vindicate = to show someone was right.

notes.punished the butler: The meaning is about the readers.

questions.q: What interested the group most afterwards?
options: the author's clever hiding of clues
questions.explain: 'Not the twist itself, but how skilfully the author had planted clues in plain sight.'

questions.q: What is the tone of the final sentence?
questions.explain: 'Admittedly, made our meetings longer, if rather more entertaining.'
